title: Overlapping subproblems in brute-force climbing stairs search
summary: When brute-force recursion splits top-down from dp[9], identical subproblems do not share results and are repeatedly expanded across different branches.
context: In the climbing stairs problem, each move climbs 1 or 2 steps, and dp[i] denotes the number of ways to reach step i. Brute-force search recursively decomposes each state using dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2] until reaching the base cases dp[1] = 1 or dp[2] = 2.
description: Computing dp[9] requires dp[8] and dp[7], and computing dp[8] again requires dp[7] and dp[6]. The two occurrences of dp[7] in the brute-force tree do not share a single computation; each occurrence is expanded and solved all over again.

The figure draws only the first four levels, with 15 state nodes in total, and 16 ellipses along the bottom indicating continued recursion down to the base cases dp[1] or dp[2]. Counts in the table (such as dp[5] appearing 4 times) cover only the four drawn levels, not the full recursion.

The tables below first list the four drawn levels and then summarize by state. Left and right subproblems in the decomposition table follow the recurrence; the children of every level-4 node are shown only as ellipses in the figure rather than drawn individually. In particular, dp[4] and dp[3] appear only on level 4, so their subproblems in those two rows come from the recurrence and are not drawn in the figure.

frames.title: Overlapping subproblems in brute-force climbing stairs search
frames.explanation: The caption at the bottom of the figure connects overlapping subproblems to exponential runtime: brute-force recursion repeatedly solves the same states, resulting in an O(2ⁿ) time bound, where 2ⁿ means 2 to the power n.
